sense: way of thinking and feeling about someone or something

terms.grammar: noun, second declension: with in or ergā and the accusative of the person
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.77.1: hōc mē animō ergā tē esse
Cic. Fam. 3.9.1: quō animō inter nōs sumus
Traupman 153: bonō animō esse, to be in a good frame of mind
terms.comment: Latin asks “in what spirit” someone is: quō animō est in nōs?, what is his attitude to us? Bonō animō esse is to be in good heart (see positive). Animus is also the mind, courage, and intention, so the phrase around it decides (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: noun, third declension: with in or ergā and the accusative
terms.comment: Will, wish; of feeling towards a person, goodwill or ill will, often with bona or mala (Lewis & Short).
The mind as thinking; for a fixed way of thinking, Morgan–Owens gives it for “attitude, mentality”. The usual Latin for feeling towards someone is animus.

evidence: Traupman 149, 274: gestus tuus mihi displicet, I don’t like your attitude
terms.comment: Traupman’s “attitude” takes the English word in its old sense, the attitude of the body: classically gestus is a bearing, posture or gesture, as of an actor or an orator (Lewis & Short), not a way of thinking.

phrases.latin: atque hoc ut tuī necessāriī sciant, hōc mē animō ergā tē esse, velim faciās eōs per litterās certiōrēs
phrases.english: and so that your friends may know that this is my attitude towards you, please let them know by letter

phrases.latin: Bonō animō es: dūcēs uxōrem hanc. — Hem. — Bonō animō es, inquam.
phrases.english: Cheer up: you’ll marry her. — What? — Cheer up, I said.
